body_markdown:
Is Carson Hocevar the next Dale Earnhardt? Absolutely. And no way.


Let me explain. Earnhardt began racing in the NASCAR Cup Series in 1975, and he won his first of seven championships in 1980, driving for Rod Osterlund. But it wasn’t until he paired up with team owner Richard Childress for a second time, in 1984, driving the No. 3 Chevrolet, that he became “The Intimidator.” And “The man in black.” And, to his detractors, “Ironhead.”


As you may be aware, Hocevar—at 23, in just his third season of Cup racing—has quickly become a legitimate sensation. Saturday night, racing at the Bristol Motor Speedway bullring in Tennessee, he wrecked Ryan Blaney, who was running second. Blaney hung around the infield until the race was over, then marched up to Hocevar, who threw the first punch, and the second, sending Blaney to the ground. Blaney jumped up and managed one good left hook before the two were separated.


Immediately, everyone forgot who won (Joey Logano), and concentrated on the fight. The TV coverage replayed the crash and the fight, from multiple angles, until we could all wince at the precise time the punches landed. ESPN, which has pointedly ignored NASCAR since it lost the rights to broadcast the races years ago, featured the fight on its *SportsCenter* show. *The New York Times,* which asked last April: “Can Carson Hocevar be the transcendent driver NASCAR has been looking for?” seems to have had that question answered. Prominent on *The Athletic,* the *Times* ’ sports website,[a top story](https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/7611732/2026/09/19/carson-hocevar-ryan-blaney-punch-nascar-bristol-playoff-race/) was “Carson Hocevar punches Ryan Blaney after contentious NASCAR Bristol playoff race,” with no mention of winner Logano.


The claustrophobic Bristol, a concrete half-mile oval surrounded by towering grandstands, is a good place for drivers’ temperatures to hit the boiling point. But we can’t overlook the pre-race comments from 77-year-old retired wrestler “Nature Boy Ric Flair,” who was being honored for being, I guess, Ric Flair. At a press conference, Flair[delivered a singleminded call to action](https://www.motorsport.com/nascar-cup/news/this-is-how-peak-nascar-comes-back/10857554/) for pissed-off drivers: “If they’re mad, they want to kick somebody’s ass, go kick it. Just make sure they take their helmet off,” he said. “Just get the helmet off and then smack them. I want to see the real emotion.”


Chris Graythen/Getty Images


Back to my thesis, then: Is Hocevar the next Dale Earnhardt, whose death in 2001 left a legion of fans without a favorite? Many of them lost interest in NASCAR. Earnhardt was unique: a working-class country boy from the South who rose through the ranks to the stratosphere, refused to take any crap from anyone, and who gained a massive number of fans who loved his take-no-prisoners attitude. Kind of like Hocevar, though he isn’t exactly a working-class country boy. And he’s from Michigan.


No, in multiple ways, he’s nothing like Dale Earnhardt, with one major exception: *His fans are exactly like Earnhardt’s were.* In their eyes, Earnhardt and Hocevar can do no wrong, and a diehard fan would be willing to spend the rent money on their drivers’ T-shirts.


Hocevar signs autographs for fans prior to the running of the NASCAR Cup Series Jack Link’s 500 on April 26, 2026, at Talladega SuperSpeedway.


Jeff Robinson/Getty Images


Hocevar, like Earnhardt did, seems to revel in sticking it to “The Man.” In Earnhardt’s time, that would have been NASCAR founder Bill France, who was succeeded by Bill France, Jr. It isn’t exactly clear who Hocevar’s “The Man” is, because NASCAR is admittedly head-over-heels about him. Arguably, his “The Man” might be the other drivers, some seen as corporate, always-polite, goody-two-shoes aghast at the fact that Hocevar has turned NASCAR into a contact sport.


Like Earnhardt did. Remember his victory at Bristol in 1999? Terry Labonte was leading the last lap when Earnhardt, in second, tapped Labonte’s car hard enough to make it spin, a wreck almost identical to Ryan Blaney’s, except Labonte took out several of the front-runners, including Tony Stewart in third and Mark Martin in fourth. Earnhardt later said he really didn’t want to spin Labonte, he only meant to—and this has become a legendary quote—“rattle his cage.” Veteran motorsports reporter Lee Spencer, in an after-hours NASCAR radio show on SiriusXM, said that “all that was missing from Hocevar’s incident was him saying he just meant to rattle Blaney’s cage. That would have been perfect.”


This fight-or-don’t argument is as old as NASCAR, and has sometimes been patently endorsed by the sanctioning body. Shortly before the 2010 NASCAR Sprint Cup season took the green flag at Daytona International Speedway, the long-defunct NASCAR Media Tour was held, where dozens of journalists descended on Charlotte, North Carolina, for a few packed days of interviews, visits to NASCAR shops, and sessions with NASCAR executives.


Circa, 1979: Track workers try to break up a fight between Cale Yarborough, Donnie Allison, and Bobby Allison, after Yarborough and Donnie Allison crashed on the final lap while battling for the lead in the Daytona 500. The incident happened before a live nationwide TV audience and is said to have spiked a huge interest in ticket sales for upcoming NASCAR races that year.


ISC Archives/CQ-Roll Call Group


It was at one of those opportunities where then-vice president of competition Robin Pemberton spoke about drivers getting into fights. “We’re going to put it back in the hands of the drivers,” Pemberton said. Followed[by a line that has become, well, infamous:](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EV9WgCEobOg&list=RDEV9WgCEobOg&start_radio=1) “Boys, have at it!”


I was there. Many of us—drivers, team owners, NASCAR officials, the media—were genuinely surprised and a little confused. Was NASCAR formally condoning fistfights and wrestling matches? Or did it go farther than that? Was it now OK to knock a car running ahead of you out of the way?


Not many drivers sought to immediately test what Pemberton meant, but plenty of NASCAR officials, including NASCAR head Brian France, tried to dial back what Pemberton said in the seasons following the comment. The most extreme example of what Pemberton might have imagined may have come in November 2015 at Martinsville Speedway; Joe Gibbs Racing driver Matt Kenseth, laps down, idled slowly around the track until the leader, Team Penske’s Joey Logano, came around. Kenseth speared Logano, sending him into the Turn 1 wall and ending his night.


It arguably wasn’t a “heat of the moment” action—a term many NASCAR teams have used to excuse something their drivers have done—because Kenseth was angry about an incident between the two a couple of weeks earlier, at Kansas Speedway, where Logano spun Kenseth out of the lead. Kenseth simply wanted payback, and he got it. And the drivers learned that too much is too much: Kenseth also got an immediate suspension and was forced to sit out the next two races, at Texas and Phoenix, returning for the season finale at Homestead-Miami Speedway. Kenseth and Logano played nice; Logano was fourth, Kenseth seventh. The late Kyle Busch, who seldom backed down from a battle, won the race and the 2015 championship.


Inarguably, it seemed inevitable that somebody would take a swing at Hocevar, whose driving style ranges from precise and proper to absolutely out of control, attempting passes in unpassable spots on track and often taking out competitors—and occasionally himself. Hocevar, typically self-appointing himself as blameless, has left a trail of tears, decorated by colorful ripped-up sheet metal.


Hocevar playing to the crowd in Bristol.


Chris Graythen/Getty Images


Still, Hocevar alone has probably tripled the value of previous-underdog Spire Racing, which entered the Cup series in 2019 after buying a NASCAR charter from the out-of-business Furniture Row Racing. Spire is owned by founder Jeff Dickerson and TWG Racing, which was founded by Mark Walter. If TWG sounds familiar, it’s probably because the company owns the Los Angeles Dodgers, and last year bought a majority stake in the Los Angeles Lakers. TWG absorbed Michael Andretti’s Andretti Global business, which led directly to ownership of the two-car Cadillac Formula 1 team Andretti fronted. Spire has two other NASCAR Cup drivers, Daniel Suarez and Michael McDowell, who are often competitive but race in the shadow cast by Hocevar and his number 77.


There’s no question Hocevar is talented and fierce, frequently dragging by sheer will a 15th-place car into the top 10. In his third year of Cup Racing, his style has only gotten more flamboyant, and any hope that he might self-police—in the way frequent-crasher Ernie Irvan did when he stood up in a drivers’ meeting and apologized, said he would do better, and then did do better—seems fleeting. I’m not waiting for Hocevar to do that.


While Earnhardt had to rely on other executives to guide his merchandise sales, Hocevar has fallen right into it. His marketing savvy is deft; Saturday night, he quickly announced that his Hocevar merchandise would be 12% off, for the next 12 hours. Why? Because Blaney’s car number is 12.


Blaney being separated from Hocevar after their coming together in the pits at Bristol over the weekend.


Chris Graythen/Getty Images


After Bristol ended, an exhausting race, almost all the drivers promptly retreated to their motorhomes, but Hocevar stuck around, shaking hands, high-fiving, and signing autographs. His popularity is unparalleled; the only driver that comes to mind who had such a quick impact on NASCAR and its fans was Tim Richmond, an IndyCar driver and Indianapolis 500 rookie of the year in 1980. The brash, good-looking, highly quotable Richmond came from money; reportedly, for his 16th birthday, his parents bought him a Pontiac Trans Am, a speedboat, *and* a Piper Cherokee airplane, which he learned to fly before his next birthday. Richmond drove for several owners in NASCAR, before landing at Hendrick Motorsports in 1986, teamed with legendary crew chief Harry Hyde.


Richmond got sick at the end of ’86 and couldn’t make the 1987 season kickoff, the Daytona 500. Supposedly he had double pneumonia, but quite a few of us knew better: Richmond had AIDS. He died in 1989, at the age of 34. We never learned how high he could soar.


Hocevar (left) and Cleetus McFarland look on during qualifying for the NASCAR Craftsman Truck Series on February 13, 2026, in Daytona Beach, Florida.


James Gilbert/Getty Images


Hocevar shows no signs of fading from the NASCAR scene—far from it. His souvenir trailer at races is absolutely mobbed. Clearly, he has benefitted (and maybe learned a thing or two) from a close friendship with[Cleetus McFarland](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/cleetus-conquers-nascar-well-in-the-sense-that-he-didnt-actually-crash/) , the professional redneck alter ego of Garrett Mitchell, who spent two years in law school before quitting to[become full-time Cleetus](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/smithology/smithology-the-cleetus-mcfactor/) . He may be the undisputed king of marketing, selling his Cleetus merchandise to his social media followers, which number[close to 5 million](https://www.youtube.com/@CleetusM) . McFarland’s friendship with former NASCAR star Greg Biffle led drag- and street-racer McFarland toward oval track competition, where he has raced in ARCA and the NASCAR Craftsman Truck and O’Reilly Auto Parts series. Hocevar and McFarland teamed up for an endurance race and seem to enjoy each other’s company, beginning last February at Daytona. They seem to be a solid one-two, if you’ll forgive the pun.


The moral of this story: If you follow motorsports at all, and you aren’t familiar with Carson Hocevar, he belongs on your radar. He is a race car driver who will be difficult ignore in seasons to come.


That’s one prediction I’m very comfortable making.
